description: let's investigate mars and the earth
summary: We studied an unexplained cone with a central depression in Utopia Planitia, Mars, near the Zhurong landing site. Using NASA’s HiRISE image and a 1 m digital terrain model, we measured its size, height and slopes in QGIS and compared it with 10 circular submarine mud volcanoes of the Kaoping margin, Taiwan, using published data. The cone’s height-to-diameter ratio (0.085) is inside the Kaoping range (0.059–0.110), and its global mean slope (about 9.7°) is almost the same as the published mean of the 13 Kaoping volcanoes (about 9.5°). A neighboring structure, with its floor below the terrain, shows that not every Martian pit is the same. We do not claim that it is a mud volcano. We show how open NASA data can turn “it looks similar” into a quantitative, reproducible comparison, and we propose a direction test for the ridges around the cone. This helps scientists form hypotheses and helps plan exploration.
details:
What it does.

It measures an unexplained Martian cone and compares it quantitatively with Earth mud volcanoes, instead of only saying “they look similar”.


How it works.

We measured the base, the central depression, the corrected height (with a regional plane fitted to eight exterior points), the slopes (489,005 pixels of a 1 m slope raster) and cross-sectional profiles. We compared dimensionless proportions with 13 published submarine mud volcanoes of Kaoping, Taiwan.


Main results.

The cone is about 791 m wide and 68 m tall. Its height/diameter (0.085) is inside the Kaoping range, and its global mean slope (9.7°) matches that of MV1 (9°). A second structure nearby has a very different shape (height/diameter 0.033, floor about 7 m below the terrain).


Benefits.

Scientists can use the numbers to test hypotheses; mission planners get slope and relief information in a region already visited by a rover; students can repeat the method with free tools.


What we hope to achieve.

A reproducible way to compare Martian structures with Earth analogs, and a test to decide if the ridges around the cone follow the cone or the regional slope.


Limitations.

No composition data; the origin of the structure is still unresolved; MV1 data are published, not measured by us.


Tools.

QGIS (Profile Tool, GDAL), HiRISE image and DTM, published data.
